title: Quantization through Dissipation and the Optical Quantum Hall Effect
authors: Zhenisbek Tagay, Ahmed Abouelkomsan, Yugo Onishi, Adbhut Gupta, Loren Pfeiffer, Liang Fu, N. P. Armitage
abstract: The integer quantum Hall effect remains the most paradigmatic and remarkable example of exact quantization in condensed matter physics. Its Hall conductivity $σ_{xy}$ is fixed to $e^2/h$ times an integer to a precision limited only by measurement and independent of disorder or interactions. This robustness has several explanations, each capturing a strikingly different piece of the physics. In Laughlin's gauge argument, flux insertion pumps an integer charge between edges, so quantization follows from gauge invariance alone. The edge-channel picture instead attributes transport to chiral, ballistic 1D channels at the sample boundary, one per filled Landau level. Bulk arguments tie $σ_{xy}$ to a topological invariant of the disordered system, with extended states compensating exactly for the current not carried by localized ones. Here we demonstrate an additional route to understanding quantization, rooted in the finite-frequency dissipative electrodynamics of the bulk. Using high-precision terahertz Faraday rotation and numerics, we show that the cyclotron resonance alone does not give quantized plateaus under Kramers-Kronig transformation. Quantization is recovered only once a faint, low-frequency, topologically enforced dissipative contribution from impurity states is included. This dynamical mechanism, hiding in plain sight within the dissipative response, ties the DC value to the finite-frequency optical response and offers a new route to quantization through the optical Hall effect.
summary: This work proposes a novel understanding of the quantized Hall conductivity by analyzing the system's finite-frequency optical response using terahertz measurements. By applying the Kramers-Kronig relation, the authors show that the quantization plateau only emerges when the low-frequency, dissipative contributions from disorder-induced impurity states are accounted for. This establishes a quantitative link between optical spectroscopy and fundamental topological transport properties.
main_problem: To establish an alternative theoretical route to understanding the exact quantization of the Hall conductivity ($\sigma_{xy}$), moving beyond standard edge-channel or topological arguments.
main_result: Quantization is recovered by including a faint, low-frequency, topologically enforced dissipative contribution from impurity states when relating the DC Hall conductivity to the finite-frequency optical response via the Kramers-Kronig relation.
method: The study combines high-precision terahertz Faraday rotation measurements (experiment) with the Kramers-Kronig integral transform and numerical calculations for disordered electron systems (theory).
model_or_system: The system is a two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) in GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures subjected to a strong magnetic field, exhibiting the Integer Quantum Hall Effect.
key_observables: Hall conductivity $\sigma_{xy}(\omega)$ (both real and imaginary parts), DC Hall conductivity $\sigma_{xy}(0)$, and the cyclotron resonance frequency ($\omega_c$).
important_parameters: Low frequency ($\omega \ll \omega_c$), low temperature (1.5 K, 4.2 K), and the presence/absence of disorder-induced impurity states.
main_assumptions: The validity of the Kramers-Kronig relation linking the DC limit to the integral over the finite-frequency spectrum, and that the low-frequency spectral weight carries the necessary topological information.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the frequency dependence of $	ext{Re}[\sigma_{xy}(\omega)]$ and $	ext{Im}[\sigma_{xy}(\omega)]$ for different mobility samples, demonstrating that the low-frequency spectral weight is crucial for reproducing the quantized DC plateau via KK reconstruction.
paper_structure: The paper first reviews the established quantization mechanisms, then details the THz measurement techniques to obtain $\sigma_{xy}(\omega)$, and finally uses the KK relation to show that only the inclusion of low-frequency, impurity-related spectral weight recovers the quantized DC plateau.
why_interesting: The explicit link between the finite-frequency optical response and the DC quantized transport coefficient provides a powerful, dynamical mechanism for understanding topological quantization, which is relevant to open quantum systems where dissipation plays a role.
